preamble: A palatalized alveolar stop [tʲ] becomes the postalveolar affricate [tʃ]. The change is typical of Goidelic. Old Irish slender t /tʲ/ became /tʃ/ in Manx, which spells it ⟨çh⟩ or ⟨ch⟩ (Old Irish tengae > çhengey 'tongue'), and is affricated to [tʃʰ] in many Scottish Gaelic dialects. In Upper Sorbian, the West Slavic soft t, written ć, is pronounced [tʃ] and has merged with č.

examples.note: Lewis, Harris and Wester Ross keep unaffricated /tʲʰ/ (/ˈtʲʰɛ̃ɣə/), so the change is dialectal.
Soft t before a front vowel gave Upper Sorbian ć, pronounced [tʃ] (also infinitives in -ć, e.g. łhać /ˈfat͡ʃ/ 'to lie'). Whether an alveolo-palatal [tɕ] stage intervened is not shown in the sources.
Church Slavonic свѣща, with the South Slavic reflex, was borrowed alongside it.
The palatal stops *ť and *ď merged with the existing č and ž.
